historical_claims.claim: CPSC publicly reported investigation of 1965-1973-era U.S. residential aluminum wiring connection hazards in 1978, with related 2003 agency followup; historical scope excludes present-day aluminum feeder performance.

evidence_claims.claim: Uniform-conductor resistance scales with resistivity and length, and inversely with cross-section
Aluminum has greater 20°C resistivity than copper so equal-resistance area is larger

supports.location: official catalogue scope of conductor materials and resistance

evidence_claims.limitations: Illustrative pure-metal ratios are not alloy-specific standardized cable dimensions.

evidence_claims.claim: Conductor electrical cross section is distinct from outside diameter, stranding and insulation

supports.location: official scope on nominal areas, solid and stranded classes

evidence_claims.limitations: Actual dimensional tolerances and stranding types depend on specific product standards.

evidence_claims.claim: Conductor resistivity commonly increases with temperature; linear alpha is a limited approximation
evidence_claims.limitations: Not valid for every temperature/material condition; fixed geometry approximation.

evidence_claims.claim: Resistance creates localized I-squared-R heating at a connection

supports.location: description of connection deterioration and heat

evidence_claims.limitations: The numeric contact-resistance example is constructed; thermal outcome needs real geometry and current.

evidence_claims.claim: Pressure contact quality and surface condition are central to conductor-terminal performance
evidence_claims.limitations: Microscopic mechanism is engineering synthesis; product-specific long-term data not independently examined.

evidence_claims.claim: Conductor alloy, size, stranding and terminal compatibility must be jointly evaluated
evidence_claims.limitations: Scope neither permits arbitrary conductor combinations nor fixes torque or crimp tool.

evidence_claims.claim: CPSC investigated overheating of 1965–1973-era aluminum residential branch wiring
evidence_claims.limitations: Historical population only; two CPSC publications are not independent authorities.

evidence_claims.claim: Older aluminum branch wiring concerns do not prove that all modern large aluminum feeders are defective

supports.location: current standards recognize Al/alloy conductor families

evidence_claims.limitations: No quantitative comparison of modern feeder reliability has been established.

evidence_claims.claim: Contact force can be affected by thermal cycling and mechanical behavior
evidence_claims.limitations: Exact creep, expansion and contact-force models require alloy/terminal research and product data.

evidence_claims.claim: Torque and compression tools must follow the evaluated connector installation method
evidence_claims.limitations: No universal torque value or connector procedure is asserted.

evidence_claims.claim: Same conductor resistance and current imply same I²R loss, not necessarily same installation suitability
evidence_claims.limitations: Heat removal, installed geometry and connection constraints not captured.
